claim: Some neurons have stimulus responses that are stable over days, whereas other neurons have highly plastic stimulus responses.
source: Some neurons have stimulus responses that are stable over days, whereas other neurons have highly plastic stimulus responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known observation that motivates the study.

claim: In a network with diverse learning rates, neurons with fast rates are more coupled to population activity than neurons with slow rates.
source: We find that, in a network with diverse learning rates, neurons with fast rates are more coupled to population activity than neurons with slow rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the network model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons with high population coupling exhibit more long-term stimulus response variability than neurons with low population coupling.
source: This plasticity-coupling link predicts that neurons with high population coupling exhibit more long-term stimulus response variability than neurons with low population coupling.
evidence: This prediction is derived from the network model and is subsequently tested with experimental data.

claim: A neuron's population coupling is correlated with the plasticity of its orientation preference in mouse visual cortex.
source: We substantiate this prediction using recordings from the Allen Brain Observatory, finding that a neuron's population coupling is correlated with the plasticity of its orientation preference.
evidence: This is validated using in vivo calcium imaging data from the Allen Brain Observatory.

claim: If a particular stimulus feature is overexpressed within an environment, more neurons will be recruited to encode this feature.
source: if a particular stimulus feature is overexpressed within an environment, for example, more neurons will be recruited to encode this feature (Sengpiel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some neurons retain highly stable preferences to specific stimuli, whereas the stimulus preference of other neurons change from day to day.
source: These recordings reveal a substantial, and puzzling, variability in the long-term stability of responses in sensory cortex: some neurons retain highly stable preferences to specific stimuli, whereas the stimulus preference of other neurons change from day to day (Ranson, 2017; Clopath et al., 2017; Poort et al., 2015; Lütcke et al., 2013; Rule et al., 2019; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Whisking responses in mouse barrel cortex are highly plastic.
source: whisking responses in mouse barrel cortex are highly plastic, whereas visual responses in mouse V1 are more stable but still exhibit fluctuations (Clopath et al., 2017; Lütcke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Visual responses in mouse V1 are more stable but still exhibit fluctuations.
source: whisking responses in mouse barrel cortex are highly plastic, whereas visual responses in mouse V1 are more stable but still exhibit fluctuations (Clopath et al., 2017; Lütcke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Sensory deprivation can induce stimulus response plasticity.
source: Moreover, it is possible to induce stimulus response plasticity through perturbations such as sensory deprivation (Rose et al., 2016), or to increase task-related stimulus response stability through rewarded learning (Poort et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Rewarded learning can increase task-related stimulus response stability.
source: Moreover, it is possible to induce stimulus response plasticity through perturbations such as sensory deprivation (Rose et al., 2016), or to increase task-related stimulus response stability through rewarded learning (Poort et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The stability of neural representation is correlated with firing rate in hippocampal place cells.
source: Although the stability of neural representation is correlated with firing rate in hippocampal place cells (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016) and in visual cortex (Ranson, 2017), it is not known how cellular or network properties influence a neuron's stimulus response stability (Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The stability of neural representation is correlated with firing rate in visual cortex.
source: Although the stability of neural representation is correlated with firing rate in hippocampal place cells (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016) and in visual cortex (Ranson, 2017), it is not known how cellular or network properties influence a neuron's stimulus response stability (Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: It is not known how cellular or network properties influence a neuron's stimulus response stability.
source: Although the stability of neural representation is correlated with firing rate in hippocampal place cells (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016) and in visual cortex (Ranson, 2017), it is not known how cellular or network properties influence a neuron's stimulus response stability (Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons with fast learning rates exhibit more variability of their stimulus selectivity than neurons with slow learning rates.
source: We find that neurons with fast learning rates exhibit more variability of their stimulus selectivity than neurons with slow learning rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Fast neurons have higher population coupling than slow neurons.
source: Intriguingly, we also find that fast neurons have higher population coupling, a measure of how correlated an individual neurons activity is with the rest of the population (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Population coupling is a measure of how correlated an individual neuron's activity is with the rest of the population.
source: Intriguingly, we also find that fast neurons have higher population coupling, a measure of how correlated an individual neurons activity is with the rest of the population (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Diverse learning rates provide a mechanism for the diverse population coupling observed in sensory cortex.
source: This unexpected plasticity-coupling link, in which more plastic neurons are also more coupled to the rest of the population, provides a mechanism for the diverse population coupling previously observed in sensory cortex (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: Strong population coupling helps plastic neurons alter their stimulus preference during a simple perceptual learning task.
source: We find that strong population coupling helps plastic neurons alter their stimulus preference during a simple perceptual learning task, but hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: Strong population coupling hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
source: We find that strong population coupling helps plastic neurons alter their stimulus preference during a simple perceptual learning task, but hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: The plasticity-coupling link ensures that highly plastic neurons are strongly coupled to the population, while less plastic neurons are weakly coupled.
source: The plasticity-coupling link exploits this dependence by ensuring that highly plastic neurons - the substrate for perceptual learning - are strongly coupled to the population, while less plastic neurons are weakly coupled and act as a stable 'backbone' of stimulus representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Less plastic neurons act as a stable 'backbone' of stimulus representation.
source: The plasticity-coupling link exploits this dependence by ensuring that highly plastic neurons - the substrate for perceptual learning - are strongly coupled to the population, while less plastic neurons are weakly coupled and act as a stable 'backbone' of stimulus representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Excitatory recurrent synapses undergo Hebbian plasticity and synaptic scaling in the network model.
source: Excitatory recurrent synapses in our network undergo Hebbian plasticity and synaptic scaling, while inhibitory synapses undergo homeostatic inhibitory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the plasticity rules implemented in the model.

claim: Inhibitory synapses undergo homeostatic inhibitory plasticity in the network model.
source: Excitatory recurrent synapses in our network undergo Hebbian plasticity and synaptic scaling, while inhibitory synapses undergo homeostatic inhibitory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the plasticity rules implemented in the model, with citation support.

claim: The learning rate is expressed postsynaptically in the network model.
source: The learning rate is expressed postsynaptically, such that the synaptic input weights onto neurons with a large α are more plastic than those with a small α (Equation 3).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model implementation.

claim: Synaptic input weights onto neurons with a large α are more plastic than those with a small α.
source: The learning rate is expressed postsynaptically, such that the synaptic input weights onto neurons with a large α are more plastic than those with a small α (Equation 3).
evidence: This describes a consequence of the model implementation.

claim: The Hebbian plasticity rule potentiates connections between neurons which share the same feedforward stimulus preference.
source: The Hebbian plasticity rule potentiates connections between neurons which share the same feedforward stimulus preference, due to their coactivity.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the plasticity rule in the model.

claim: Strong bidirectional connections emerge amongst stimulus-specific groups of neurons.
source: This drives the emergence of strong bidirectional connections amongst stimulus-specific groups of neurons, while the remaining non-specific connections weaken (Figure 1B,C; Ko et al., 2013; Clopath et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in figures and supported by citations.

claim: Non-specific connections weaken during plasticity in the network model.
source: This drives the emergence of strong bidirectional connections amongst stimulus-specific groups of neurons, while the remaining non-specific connections weaken (Figure 1B,C; Ko et al., 2013; Clopath et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in figures and supported by citations.

claim: Fast neurons develop strong, specific connections sooner than slow neurons.
source: Fast neurons develop these strong, specific connections sooner than slow neurons (Figure 1B, solid lines).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Increased learning rate leads to stronger synaptic weight fluctuations.
source: However, the increased learning rate also leads to stronger synaptic weight fluctuations.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations.

claim: For slow neurons, non-specific and specific connections tend towards either zero or the maximum synaptic weights respectively.
source: For slow neurons, in contrast, non-specific and specific connections tend towards either zero or the maximum synaptic weights respectively, remaining relatively stable after convergence (Figure 1B, black lines).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Connection specificity is stronger and more stable for slow neurons compared with fast neurons.
source: This leads to connection specificity that is stronger and more stable compared with fast neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increasing α predominantly drives an increase in non-specific connections rather than a decrease in specific connections.
source: Increasing α predominantly drives an increase in non-specific connections rather than a decrease in specific connections.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations with diverse learning rates.

claim: Increasing α leads to an overall increase in the amount of synaptic input amongst neurons with high α.
source: This leads to an overall increase in the amount of synaptic input amongst neurons with high α.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations.

claim: Population coupling is correlated with the amount of local synaptic input in cortical networks.
source: Since population coupling is correlated with the amount of local synaptic input in cortical networks (Okun et al., 2015), this measure could be a useful and experimentally observable proxy for the specificity of recurrent connectivity in our networks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Population coupling increases with learning rate in the network model.
source: Interestingly, population coupling increases with learning rate, closely following the dependence of non-specific connectivity on α (Figure 1E, red points).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A strong plasticity-coupling link requires both moderate amounts of noise within the network and relatively slow synaptic scaling compared with Hebbian plasticity.
source: A strong plasticity-coupling link requires both moderate amounts of noise within the network and relatively slow synaptic scaling compared with Hebbian plasticity, in agreement with experimental data (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This is determined from parameter exploration in the model and supported by citation.

claim: Networks with diverse learning rates develop strong synaptic connections between neurons with similar receptive fields.
source: Both networks with uniform α and networks with diverse α develop strong synaptic connections between neurons with similar receptive fields.
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations.

claim: There is a broader range of summed synaptic inputs in diverse networks compared with uniform networks.
source: There is, however, a broader range of summed synaptic inputs in diverse networks, when compared with uniform networks (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The total excitatory synaptic input onto a neuron covaries with α in the diverse network.
source: This occurs because the total excitatory synaptic input onto a neuron covaries with α in the diverse network (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The population coupling of a neuron is determined by its total excitatory synaptic input in networks with diverse α.
source: In agreement with our previous observations, the population coupling of a neuron is determined by its total excitatory synaptic input in networks with diverse α (Figure 2C, blue line. r = 0.29, p<1e-5, Spearman correlation).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations with statistical analysis.

claim: Diverse learning rates within a cortical network lead to a broad distribution of population coupling.
source: Diverse learning rates within a cortical network indeed lead to a broad distribution of population coupling, as observed by Okun et al. (2015); Figure 2D, blue).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and matches experimental observations.

claim: In networks with uniform α, a neuron's population coupling is not correlated with the amount of synaptic input it receives.
source: Although the network with uniform α also exhibits some heterogeneity of population coupling, in this network a neuron's population coupling is not correlated with the amount of synaptic input it receives (Figure 2C,D, green. p=0.52, Spearman correlation).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations with statistical analysis.

claim: Networks with diverse learning rates better match experimental observations than networks with uniform learning rates.
source: This suggests that networks with diverse learning rates better match experimental observations than networks with uniform learning rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing model results with experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of stimulus selectivity fluctuations is independent of population coupling in the uniform network.
source: We find that the magnitude of these fluctuations is independent of population coupling in the uniform network (p=0.4, Spearman correlation), but is correlated with population coupling in the diverse network (r = 0.18, p=1e-5, Spearman correlation Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations with statistical analysis.

claim: The magnitude of stimulus selectivity fluctuations is correlated with population coupling in the diverse network.
source: We find that the magnitude of these fluctuations is independent of population coupling in the uniform network (p=0.4, Spearman correlation), but is correlated with population coupling in the diverse network (r = 0.18, p=1e-5, Spearman correlation Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the receptive-field based network simulations with statistical analysis.

claim: The majority of excitatory synaptic input received by neurons in visual cortex is recurrent.
source: As the majority of excitatory synaptic input received by neurons in visual cortex is recurrent, we simulate a regime with relatively weak feedforward stimulus-related input and high noise for Figure 2A-E (Cossell et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Networks with diverse α exhibit a broader distribution of population coupling compared to networks with uniform α.
source: This results in a broader distribution of population coupling and weaker stimulus selectivity for networks with diverse α, compared to networks with uniform α (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations across different noise levels.

claim: Networks with diverse α exhibit weaker stimulus selectivity compared to networks with uniform α.
source: This results in a broader distribution of population coupling and weaker stimulus selectivity for networks with diverse α, compared to networks with uniform α (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations across different noise levels.

claim: Diverse learning rates introduce a correlation between a neuron's population coupling and its total excitatory synaptic input.
source: Moreover, diverse learning rates introduce a correlation between a neuron's population coupling and its total excitatory synaptic input, in agreement with experimental observations (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and matches experimental observations.

claim: Roughly 75% of neurons express variability of their preferred orientation or direction between the beginning and the end of the experiment.
source: Roughly 75% of neurons express variability of their preferred orientation or direction between the beginning and the end of the experiment.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data.

claim: Population coupling is weakly but significantly correlated with the average change in preferred orientation.
source: Population coupling is weakly but significantly correlated with the average change in preferred orientation and in preferred direction (Figure 3E, r = 0.1, p<1e-5 and r = 0.12, p<1e-5, Spearman correlation).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data with statistical analysis.

claim: Population coupling is weakly but significantly correlated with the average change in preferred direction.
source: Population coupling is weakly but significantly correlated with the average change in preferred orientation and in preferred direction (Figure 3E, r = 0.1, p<1e-5 and r = 0.12, p<1e-5, Spearman correlation).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data with statistical analysis.

claim: The majority of experiments show a trend in which neurons with plastic orientation preferences have a higher mean population coupling than those with stable orientation or direction preferences.
source: While there is substantial variability of the strength of the effect, the majority of experiments show a trend in which neurons with plastic orientation preferences have a higher mean population coupling than those with stable orientation or direction preferences (Figure 3F, p<0.001 for both static and drifting gratings, t-test).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data with statistical analysis.

claim: There is no dependence of the tendency of an individual neuron to change stimulus preference on its average calcium fluorescence.
source: As the mean activity level of a neuron could conceivably determine its stimulus preference stability (Ranson, 2017; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016), we tested this and found no dependence of the tendency of a individual neuron to change stimulus preference on its average calcium fluorescence (p=0.88, Spearman correlation, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is tested in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data with statistical analysis.

claim: Population coupling is anti-correlated with orientation selectivity in the Allen Brain Observatory dataset.
source: In agreement with our network model, and in contrast with observations from Okun et al. (2015), population coupling is anti-correlated with orientation selectivity in the Allen Brain Observatory dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of Allen Brain Observatory data.

claim: A network with only fast α quickly learns the stimulus associations.
source: We find that a network with only fast α quickly learns the stimulus associations (Figure 4A, bottom).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: Repeated associations with neurons that do not share feedforward stimuli cause the specificity of recurrent connectivity to decrease in networks with only fast α.
source: However, repeated associations with neurons that do not share feedforward stimuli cause the specificity of recurrent connectivity to decrease, thus degrading the representation of feedforward stimuli (Figure 4A, top).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: The network with only slow α retains a stable representation of the feedforward stimuli but performs poorly in representing the associated stimulus.
source: Conversely, the network with only slow α retains a stable representation of the feedforward stimuli but performs poorly in representing the associated stimulus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: The network with diverse α has fast neurons which flexibly learn stimulus associations and slow neurons which maintain a 'backbone' of stimulus representation.
source: The network with diverse α overcomes these issues by having fast neurons which flexibly learn stimulus associations and slow neurons which maintain a 'backbone' of stimulus representation (see diagram, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Strongly coupling the plastic neuron to the population improves perceptual learning performance.
source: We find that strongly coupling the plastic neuron to the population improves performance, while strongly coupling the static neurons to the population impairs performance (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations with a single plastic neuron.

claim: Strongly coupling the static neurons to the population impairs perceptual learning performance.
source: We find that strongly coupling the plastic neuron to the population improves performance, while strongly coupling the static neurons to the population impairs performance (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations with a single plastic neuron.

claim: The new stimulus association is learned only when there is low population coupling amongst static neurons and high population coupling for the plastic neuron.
source: These two effects combine, such that the new stimulus association is learned only when there is low population coupling amongst static neurons (PCstatic) and high population coupling for the plastic neuron (PCplastic) (Figure 4D, labelled Φ).
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations with a single plastic neuron.

claim: A network with diverse α advantageously combines properties of networks with only slow α and only fast α for stimulus decoding.
source: A network with diverse α seems to advantageously combine both of these properties, so that its performance is high across the entire range of input strength and noise levels.
evidence: This is observed in the stimulus decoding simulations.

claim: Tracking of hippocampal cell assemblies reveal subsets of either plastic, highly active neurons or rigid, less active neurons.
source: In particular, tracking of hippocampal cell assemblies reveal subsets of either plastic, highly active neurons or rigid, less active neurons (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Neurons in primary visual cortex exhibit characteristic fluctuations of their stimulus selectivity during baseline measurements.
source: In primary visual cortex - which we model - neurons exhibit characteristic fluctuations of their stimulus selectivity during baseline measurements, but nonetheless tend to retain their preferred stimulus following recovery from sensory deprivation (Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Neurons tend to retain their preferred stimulus following recovery from sensory deprivation.
source: In primary visual cortex - which we model - neurons exhibit characteristic fluctuations of their stimulus selectivity during baseline measurements, but nonetheless tend to retain their preferred stimulus following recovery from sensory deprivation (Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The population coupling of a neuron is correlated across brain states.
source: Since the population coupling of a neuron is correlated across brain states, and is only weakly dependent on stimulus type and mean fluorescence, we believe that it provides a good measure of a neurons functional integration within the local network, and would - according to our model - therefore provide a reasonable estimate of its propensity for perceptual learning (Figure 4D; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017; Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Population coupling is only weakly dependent on stimulus type and mean fluorescence.
source: Since the population coupling of a neuron is correlated across brain states, and is only weakly dependent on stimulus type and mean fluorescence, we believe that it provides a good measure of a neurons functional integration within the local network, and would - according to our model - therefore provide a reasonable estimate of its propensity for perceptual learning (Figure 4D; Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017; Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Significant changes in synaptic efficacies can be expressed within 62 minutes.
source: Nonetheless, significant changes in synaptic efficacies can be expressed within this time (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The network model provides a parsimonious explanation for the diverse population coupling observed in sensory cortex.
source: Our network model provides a parsimonious explanation for the diverse population coupling recently observed in sensory cortex (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results in relation to experimental observations.

claim: Population coupling is dependent on the amount of recurrent synaptic input a neuron receives.
source: Population coupling is dependent on the amount of recurrent synaptic input a neurons receives, in agreement with experimental data (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and matches experimental observations.

claim: The width of the population coupling distribution increases as the recurrent network approaches a dynamic regime dominated by high noise and diverse selectivity.
source: Moreover, the width of the population coupling distribution increases as the recurrent network approaches a dynamic regime dominated by high noise and diverse selectivity, typical in cortical networks (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations across different parameter regimes.

claim: In order to enhance perceptual learning, plastic neurons in recurrent networks should be more coupled to the rest of the population than stable neurons.
source: The functional impact of population coupling on learning is crucial: in order to enhance perceptual learning, plastic neurons in recurrent networks should be more coupled to the rest of the population than stable neurons (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: High population coupling helps plastic neurons change their stimulus preference towards an associated stimulus.
source: We find that high population coupling helps plastic neuron change their stimulus preference towards an associated stimulus, but hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: High population coupling hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
source: We find that high population coupling helps plastic neuron change their stimulus preference towards an associated stimulus, but hinders the ability of stable neurons to provide an instructive signal for learning.
evidence: This is observed in the perceptual learning simulations.

claim: Correlated diversity of population coupling and learning rate enables both robust stimulus representation and a flexible substrate suitable for perceptual learning.
source: Correlated diversity of population coupling and learning rate therefore enables both robust stimulus representation (low α, PC) and a flexible substrate suitable for perceptual learning (high α, PC).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined model results.

claim: The plasticity-coupling link efficiently combines stable and flexible stimulus representation.
source: Based on our findings we propose that the plasticity-coupling link efficiently combines stable and flexible stimulus representation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the model results and experimental validation.
